chapter_theme: Ainkurunuru 321 to 330, Othalanthaiyar's paalai decade on the middle of the waste (இடைச்சுரப் பத்து): in every poem the man, on the burning road away from the girl, sets the cruelty of the land against her nature (பண்பு, குணன்), which cools the heat, travels with him, takes his heart and at last turns him back.

321.reading: Crossing a burning forest where the chisel-beaked hen of the dry-headed kite climbs the fork of the omai tree and calls out in loneliness, the man says that though he passes many hills where the language changes, the good nature of the girl with bright bangles does not leave him.
321.nuance: The distance is measured in languages, not miles (மொழிபெயர்): he has left the land where her speech is spoken, and still what stays with him is her nature (குணனே), not her face.

thinai_evidence.note: the kite on the omai in a land the heat burns is the dry waste

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade; inferred from the poem: the man on the road speaks to himself of the girl he left, naming her by her bangles

iraicchi.act: the hen kite, alone on the bare fork, calls out for its mate
iraicchi.sense: the lonely call on his road is the call of the woman he has left behind, which is why her nature does not leave him however far he goes

322.reading: The man tells the road through the waste that before, when summer lingered, the tall bamboo withered and the fierce sun scorched the rock, it was hot; now, each time he thinks of the girl with the bright forehead, the path has become cool.
322.nuance: The weather has not changed: முன்னே and இனியே divide the same road by his thought, not by the season, so memory of her is made the one thing stronger than the paalai sun.

thinai_evidence.note: the lingering summer that splits the rock and the waste road fix paalai

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade; inferred from the poem: the man addresses the waste road itself (வெய்ய வாயினை), contrasting its heat before with its coolness now

323.reading: The man tells his heart that what came with him across the forking roads of the hot waste, where a strong-toothed red dog watches for a boar among the cactus for his craving pregnant mate, is the nature of the girl it desired.

thinai_evidence.note: the red dog and the cactus of the hot waste are paalai things

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade; inferred from the poem: the closing words address the heart (நெஞ்சம் நீ நயந்தோள்)

iraicchi.act: the male red dog hunts for his pregnant mate who craves food
iraicchi.sense: the male providing for his mate is what the man has gone out to do, and seeing it he finds her nature, not the errand, has travelled with him

324.reading: On the long road where the summer heat has eaten everything like fire, the man says that if he closes his eyes even a little he will surely see, in the great house in the dead of night, the dark girl with spreading hair whose beauty spots outdo the vengai blossom.
324.nuance: The dream is placed exactly: not her in general but her in the house at midnight (நள்ளென் கங்குல் நளிமனை), so the man's longing is for the home life the road has interrupted. The certainty (காண்குவென் மன்ற) is his; whether the dream holds is not asked.

thinai_evidence.note: the summer heat on the long road fixes paalai; the night and the house are where his dream goes

comparisons.tenor: the beauty spots on her skin

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade; inferred from the poem: the man speaks to himself of the sleep he can snatch on the road

325.reading: The man says the hard waste of scorching heat, where a bird, frightened by the rattle of leaves on the summer peepal, does not go in to feed and flies off to another land, does not harm him, for he has the nature of his beloved as his companion.
325.nuance: The bird gives up and goes elsewhere because the place frightens it; the man, who has also gone elsewhere, says he is not harmed because he does not travel alone. A reader may hear the bird as the man who left; it does nothing a lover should do here, so it stays scene. Line 2's புகாவுண்ணாது is read here as not going in to eat.

thinai_evidence.note: summer and the hard waste fix paalai

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade; inferred from the poem: the man speaks of himself (எம்வெம் காதலி) on the road

326.reading: In the broad land where the blaze shimmers, where a young doe with her fawn withers for want of any shade and the path never fills because its water has been cut off, the man says the waste is truly cruel, yet sweet is the nature of the girl he left behind.
326.nuance: The poem is built on இன்னா against இனிய: the waste is harsh, her nature is sweet. The doe withering with her fawn could be read as the woman at home, but she only suffers and does nothing a person of the situation does, so it stays scene. மறையான் in line 5 is hard: perhaps that she stayed behind in secret or out of sight.

thinai_evidence.note: the blazing land and the waterless road are paalai

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade; inferred from the poem: the man sets the cruel road against the girl he left

327.reading: On the high-bamboo waste where the groves are withered by the sun and a small-eyed elephant, afraid its spotted trunk will burn, will not touch the ground, the man says that even in such a hard place the nature of this fine girl has made things cool.
327.nuance: The elephant, the largest creature, holds its trunk off the ground for fear of burning; the coolness the man claims is measured against that.

thinai_evidence.note: the sun-withered groves of the waste are paalai

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade; inferred from the poem: the man speaks of this girl (இத் தகையோள்) as present to his mind on the road

328.reading: The man says that though the forest of ripe-musth groves he has crossed is cool, with light rain falling and fragrant flowers strewn, it is truly hot for him, since he has left behind his gentle sweet companion.
328.nuance: The decade's other poems have her memory cool the hot road; this one reverses it, and a road the rain has cooled burns because she is not with him. Paalai here is a state of the man, not of the land.

thinai_evidence.note: the man has left her and crossed the forest; the separation, not the weather, makes it paalai

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade; inferred from the poem: the man speaks of himself (இறந்தேற்கே) who has crossed the forest

329.reading: Having crossed the vast ruined land where no one goes and the hard waste of hostile frontiers, the man wonders whether his strong heart will come back with him, the heart taken by the girl who stayed behind with her close-fitting bangles slipping off.
329.nuance: The heart is called strong (உரங்கெழு), the strength that let him leave, yet she has kept it; the slipping bangles are the sign at home of what the road costs.

thinai_evidence.note: the ruined, peopleless waste is paalai

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade; inferred from the poem: the man speaks of his own heart (என் உரங்கெழு நெஞ்சே), which she has taken; whether he addresses it or his companions (நம்மொடு) the poem leaves open

330.reading: Though they have come through the sun-scorched forest gone to hot dust, the man says the journey should stop now, for the girl with bright bangles, her eyes wet with weeping and her beauty ruined, keeps thinking in her heart of the scorching waste he is crossing.
330.nuance: The decade's last poem turns him back. What stops him is not the road but her picture of the road: she suffers his journey in her mind (உள்ளத்துப் படரே), so his going is her pain.

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade; inferred from the poem: the man, partway through the journey (வந்தனம் ஆயினும்), resolves to give it up; this is the situation of செலவழுங்குதல்

links.note: The Kural's man says the fire she gives burns when he moves away from her (நீங்கின் தெறூஉம்); Ainkurunuru 322's man, far from her on the summer road, says the thought of her makes the burning path cool (தண்ணிய).
links.teaches: Held together they give opposite laws for distance: in the couplet absence from her is the source of heat, while in the desert poem absence is already given and her remembered presence is the only coolness, so whether she burns or cools depends on whether the man is measuring his desire or the land.

links.note: In 322 thinking of her turns a hot road cool; in 328 a road cooled by rain and flowers is hot because he has left her.
links.teaches: The two poems of one decade run the same switch in both directions, so the poet shows that paalai heat is set by her presence or absence in the man's mind and can override real rain as easily as real sun.

links.note: Akananuru 5's colophon has the man give up the journey (செலவழுங்கியது) at the sight of her tearful face before he sets out; in Ainkurunuru 330 he has already crossed the scorching forest (வந்தனம் ஆயினும்) when he calls off the journey (ஒழிகஇனிச் செலவே) thinking of her weeping eyes.
links.teaches: The pair shows that giving up the journey is not tied to a moment: the tears seen at the doorstep in Akananuru 5 and the tears only imagined halfway in Ainkurunuru 330 do the same work, so in this situation her grief, present or pictured, is what overrules the errand, not the danger of the road.

links.note: In Akananuru 19 the man reproaches a heart that neither stayed with her nor crosses the hills with him; in Ainkurunuru 329 he says the heart was taken by her and wonders whether it will come back with him.
links.teaches: Read together they show two accounts of the traveller's divided heart: the Akananuru man blames it for wavering between her and the road, while the Ainkurunuru man concedes it never left her, so the reproach of Akananuru 19 becomes in the short poem a plain admission that he travels heartless.

links.note: Both men, on the burning road, see the girl in sleep; Ainkurunuru 324 says he will surely see her (காண்குவென் மன்ற), while Akananuru 39 calls the dream false (வாய்அல் கனவின்) because it left his hand empty.
links.teaches: The short poem gives only the traveller's confidence in the dream, and the long one tells how it ends on waking, so together they show the road-dream as both his comfort and his torment, and explain why the returned man of Akananuru 39 can answer her charge of forgetting with it.

links.note: In Akananuru 197 the friend comforts the woman with the image of a tusker embracing his pregnant mate on the man's road; in Ainkurunuru 323 the man himself crosses a road where a red dog hunts for his craving pregnant mate.
links.teaches: The friend's reassurance rests on an assumption that the man will see such creatures and remember, and Ainkurunuru 323 shows it from his side: he does see the male caring for its mate and finds the girl's nature has come with him, so the comfort offered at home is confirmed by the road.

links.note: In Kuruntokai 285 the waiting woman asks where he can be, who crossed sky-high hills where a lone kite sits on the nyemai top; in Ainkurunuru 321 the man on such hills hears the hen kite call from the omai and says her nature never leaves him.
links.teaches: The same bare tree and kite are imagined by the woman and actually met by the man, and the pair answers her question from the other end of the road: where she fears he has forgotten her, the same scene brings her back to him.

links.note: The Kural's man says love is sweeter than toddy because merely thinking of it brings unfailing joy; in Ainkurunuru 325 the man says the scorching waste does not harm him because he has her nature as companion.
links.teaches: The couplet states that remembered love never fails to give joy, and the Ainkurunuru puts that claim to a hard test, the peopleless summer waste, where the memory works as a travelling companion (துணை), so the maxim gains a situation in which its truth is a matter of survival.
